title: "Per Pupil Spending and Incarceration Rates Across U.S. States"
author: "Logan Utter"

## Data

This analysis uses panel data covering all 50 U.S. states from 2011 through 2021, giving 550 state-year observations. The dependent variable is the incarceration rate per 100,000 residents, drawn from the Bureau of Justice Statistics. Independent variables come from the National Center for Education Statistics (per-pupil spending, high school graduation rates), FRED (median household income), the Census Bureau (poverty rate, Gini coefficient), the FBI UCR program (law enforcement officers), the Kids Count Data Center (single-parent households), and the National Governors Association (governor party).

d <- read.csv("data/incarceration data.csv")

The raw CSV contains blank rows and two empty columns picked up from the original Excel spreadsheet. Both are removed before analysis. 

d <- d[!is.na(d$Year), ]
d$X <- NULL
d$X.1 <- NULL

Median household income and per-pupil spending are stored as text in the raw file because their values contain commas. Both are converted to numeric.

d$Median.Household.Income.... <- as.numeric(gsub("[ ,]", "", d$Median.Household.Income....))
d$Per.Pupil.Spending..... <- as.numeric(gsub("[ ,]", "", d$Per.Pupil.Spending.....))

The percentage-based variables (high school graduation rate, poverty rate, single-parent households, and the Gini coefficient) are stored as decimals but reported here as percentages, so each is multiplied by 100. This makes the corresponding coefficients interpretable as the effect of a one percentage point change.

d$High.School.Graduation.Rate.... <- d$High.School.Graduation.Rate.... * 100
d$Poverty.Rate.... <- d$Poverty.Rate.... * 100
d$Children.Living.in.Single.Parent.Households.... <- d$Children.Living.in.Single.Parent.Households.... * 100
d$Gini.Index <- d$Gini.Index * 100

R converts spaces and punctuation from the original headers into periods, so column names are shortened for readability. Rows are sorted by state and year.

names(d) <- c("year", "state", "incr", "hsg", "mhi", "gp",
              "pr", "pps", "sph", "pey", "gc", "leo")

d <- d[order(d$state, d$year), ]

str(d)

## Summary Statistics

Before estimating the model, the distribution of each variable and its bivariate relationship with the incarceration rate are examined.

summary(d[, 3:12])

Pairwise correlations between the incarceration rate and each independent variable show the direction and strength of each relationship before controlling for other factors.

round(cor(d$incr, d[, 4:12]), 4)

The scatter plot of incarceration rate against per-pupil spending helps illustrate the bivariate relationship between our dependent variable and our main variable of interest.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(d, aes(x = pps, y = incr)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
labs(
  x = "Per-pupil spending ($)",
  y = "Incarceration rate per 100,000 residents",
  title = "Incarceration and per-pupil spending, U.S. states 2011-2021"
)

Poverty rate had the highest correlation coefficient among the independent variables. This bivariate relationship can be observed in the scatter plot below.

ggplot(d, aes(x = pr, y = incr)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
labs(
  x = "Poverty rate (%)",
  y = "Incarceration rate per 100,000 residents",
  title = "Incarceration and poverty rate, U.S. states 2011-2021"
)
